text.p: Here are the leading stories in the Belgrade press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Domestic producers are increasingly protesting against what they see as excessive, unnecessary and low-quality imports. They complain that this is affecting their sales, draining the country of hard currency and inflating its trade gap. Chairman of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce Vlajko Stojiljkovic calls for stricter protective quality control.
- Montenegro plans to woo foreign capital for the construction of power stations. Its government is drafting tender papers to be published abroad.

- Bosnian Serbs did not participate in the drafting of the "special relations" accord with Yugoslavia. A Republika Srpska delegation member tells Nasa Borba that the background of the document is "much more sinister for us than can be guessed" and that Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic insisted it be signed at the height of the post-election crisis in Serbia. Head of the RS delegation Momcilo Krajisnik quotes Milosevic as saying that "all those who have written me off prematurely are in for a surprise".

- Loss of principal media could spell doom to Milosevic's position as leader. He is unlikely to allow any major democratization in Serbian Radio Television, Tanjug news agency and Politika daily, at least not before the next elections.

- Jurists are divided as to whether Montenegro can become a member of the International Monetary Fund. Under the federal Constitution Parliament decides on accession to international organizations but republics also "may join international organizations" on the basis of unspecified prerogatives.
